  # Document Analysis: covid2.pdf
  
  **Document:** NBER Working Paper No. 27392, "The Impact of COVID-19 on Student Experiences and Expectations: Evidence from a Survey" by Esteban M. Aucejo, Jacob F. French, Maria Paola Ugalde Araya, and Basit Zafar (National Bureau of Economic Research, June 2020).
  
  ## Overview
  This is an academic working paper (not peer-reviewed) presenting the first systematic survey-based analysis of COVID-19's effects on higher education. Researchers surveyed ~1,500 undergraduate students at Arizona State University (ASU) in late April 2020, using a design that elicited both actual (post-COVID) and counterfactual (no-COVID) outcomes from each respondent to compute subjective individual-level treatment effects. The paper covers academic outcomes (graduation, GPA, major choice, study habits, online learning preference) and labor-market outcomes (current employment, wages, future job/earnings expectations), and examines heterogeneity by income, race, first-generation status, gender, and Honors status, plus the mediating role of financial and health shocks.
  
  ## Key Findings — Societal/Business/Well-being Impact
  - Large negative academic effects: 13% delayed graduation, 11% withdrew from a class, 12% changed major intentions; ~50% reported decreased study hours and decreased academic performance.
  - Large labor-market disruption: 40% of students lost a job, internship, or job offer; working students saw a 31% drop in wages and 37% drop in hours worked; 61% reported a family member lost income or a job.
  - Forward-looking/well-being impact: 29% expect to earn less at age 35; perceived probability of finding a job before graduation fell by about 20% (13 percentage points); expected earnings at 35 declined ~2.3-2.5%, suggesting students expect long-lasting harm.
  - Socioeconomic inequality theme: effects were highly unequal — lower-income students 55% more likely to delay graduation, 41% more likely to report major-choice impact, and experienced nearly double the pre-existing GPA gap versus richer peers.
  - Health and financial shocks (used as proxies for pandemic-era "well-being" stress) are shown to statistically explain a substantial share (up to ~40-70%) of these disparate academic/economic outcomes between income groups.
  - Overall conclusion: COVID-19 substantially and unevenly disrupted college students' academic and economic trajectories, worsening pre-existing socioeconomic achievement gaps, with policy implications that addressing economic/health burdens could mitigate widening inequality.
